findings.finding: The `git archive FETCH_HEAD | tar -x -C <fresh repo>` pipeline the plan prescribes for materialising the orphan tickets branch into the isolated repo does not specify `--strip-components` or the exact path prefix the tickets branch tree root contains. If the tree root of the `tickets` orphan branch is `.tickets-tracker/` (the gitignored store directory), `git archive` will produce paths like `.tickets-tracker/…` and the extract will land correctly. But if the tree root is the repo root (containing `.tickets-tracker/` as a subdirectory among other things committed to `tickets`), the extract in the fresh repo would place unexpected files alongside the store directory. The plan does not specify what the tickets branch tree actually looks like, so the implementer cannot confidently write the pipeline.
findings.location: Isolation section: 'HOW the content is obtained … git archive FETCH_HEAD | tar -x -C <fresh repo>'
findings.suggested_fix: If the tickets branch tree root is the repo root (most likely, since `rebar init` commits to the repo root on the orphan branch), use `git archive FETCH_HEAD | tar -x -C <fresh_repo>` directly — no strip needed. Confirm by running `git ls-tree FETCH_HEAD` in the source checkout and add that observation to the CI step comment.

findings.finding: The idempotence criterion says 'a repeated pass after each direction writes nothing' — 'each direction' is ambiguous between (a) one repeated pass after all inbound mutations together and one after all outbound mutations together, or (b) one repeated pass after each individual mutation. If interpretation (a), a mutation that is not individually idempotent could be masked when its effect is overwritten by a later mutation in the suite before the idempotence check runs.

findings.suggested_fix: In the test helpers that invoke the reconciler, use `subprocess.run([...], timeout=120, check=True, capture_output=True)`; document the timeout value in `tests/external/live_jira_dc/README.md` alongside the isolation contract.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a preflight assertion in the seeding fixture that `len(seeded_keys) >= 2 * observed_page_size + 1` BEFORE running any reconciler pass, and fail fast with a diagnostic message if the target was not reached, so partial seeding failure is caught rather than silently weakening the pagination coverage.

findings.finding: The seeding fixture issues `2*observed+1` sequential `dc_transport.create_issue` calls with no error handling for partial failure. If some calls fail (harness transient error, rate limit, resource exhaustion), `seeded_keys` is silently smaller than required — the pagination assertion (`recovered_count == len(seeded_keys)`) then passes trivially on whatever subset succeeded, without detecting that fewer than three pages were ever exercised.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Document a retry policy for proving-read REST calls in the `dc_mutations` helper (e.g., up to 3 attempts with exponential backoff starting at 0.5 s) and apply it consistently across all oracle reads, so transient harness HTTP errors are retried before the cell is failed.

findings.finding: No retry or backoff is specified for any of the REST API calls made during the 28+ mutation-and-proving-read cells (inbound and outbound). The harness is a Docker container on CI infrastructure; transient HTTP failures (connection reset, 503 from a momentarily overloaded container) will cause a mutation cell to fail with no recovery, making the suite flaky and masking legitimate regressions behind noise.
findings.location: AC oracle table (rows 1-14 for both inbound and outbound); 'dc_mutations helper' in Scope section
scenarios: The Docker container's GC pauses or the Linux bridge interface hiccups for 200 ms; a `GET /rest/api/2/issue/{key}` proving-read returns a connection error; the cell fails; the CI run is marked red for a network transient rather than a code defect.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Define the DC harness container lifecycle (fresh-per-run guarantee or explicit pre-run teardown of all test-created issues) and add a pytest fixture `autouse` teardown that deletes issues in `seeded_keys` and any mutation-created issues, so the retire path is specified and tested regardless of container persistence.
evidence: "Seed via `dc_transport.create_issue` in a pytest fixture … collecting the returned keys into a `seeded_keys` set."
"After the inbound pass, `recovered_count` is the number of `seeded_keys` for which a local ticket exists"
No mention of fixture teardown, container-freshness guarantee, or issue deletion after the run.
T9 checklist: 'There is a RETIRE/cleanup path — it doesn't leak/accumulate.'
findings.finding: The plan never specifies the lifecycle of DC-side issues created during testing (pagination seeding via `dc_transport.create_issue` and per-mutation fixtures). It collects `seeded_keys` but defines no retire/cleanup path. If the Dockerized Jira container persists across CI runs (e.g. on a self-hosted runner or a cached service container), accumulated issues from prior runs inflate the observed issue count, corrupt pagination-seeding assertions (the '2 * observed + 1' threshold is met before the current run seeds anything), and leave stale bindings that interact with a fresh store copy.
findings.location: "volume — and note WHAT drives it" bullet; AC bullet: "the effective server page size is OBSERVED and reported…"
scenarios: Self-hosted runner with a persistent Docker service container: second CI run finds 2*N+1 pre-existing issues from run 1 before seeding, so the pagination threshold is satisfied by stale data and the seeding assertion counts only the new keys — the recovered_count assertion passes while the pagination exercise is illusory.
Ephemeral runner where the container IS fresh: no observable breakage, but the plan provides no mechanism to confirm freshness, so the reader cannot tell which regime they are in.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a session-scoped `autouse` fixture that yields after seeding and deletes all keys in `seeded_keys` plus any keys created by mutation fixtures in a `finally` block. In the CI workflow, document (or enforce via a health-check step) whether the service container is fresh per job or shared across runs.

findings.finding: Row 14's inbound oracle is self-referential and non-executable: 'assert the state the probe actually produces, read from the same JSON' says nothing about WHAT to assert. The reconciler's absence-probe action may mark a ticket as absent/archived, leave it deleted from the local store, or set a status field — an executor cannot write a concrete test without knowing which outcome is expected and what `rebar show` returns for an absence-probed ticket.
findings.location: Acceptance criteria oracle table, Row 14, inbound oracle column
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the current oracle text with a concrete assertion: e.g., '`rebar show <local_id>` exits with a non-zero code (ticket removed from local store) AND the binding store no longer maps the key' — or whichever outcome the reconciler actually produces, as confirmed by reading `_apply_inbound_probe` in the source.

findings.finding: The oracle for the `delete` mutation (row 14) is specified as 'assert the state the probe actually produces, read from the same JSON' — which is the self-authored-oracle / change-detector anti-pattern. Rather than pre-specifying WHAT the absence path's observable state SHOULD BE (e.g. ticket file absent, or ticket carries a `deleted: true` field, or binding is removed from bindings.json), the criterion instructs the test to observe whatever the probe produces and assert that. A test written to this spec would pass even if the probe left the ticket in a stale/incorrect state, because it asserts the actual outcome rather than the expected one.
findings.location: Acceptance criteria — oracle table, row 14 (delete mutation)
findings.suggested_fix: Name the specific condition that proves the absence path ran correctly. For example: after the inbound pass following DC deletion, `rebar show <local_id>` exits non-zero (ticket not found) OR the ticket JSON carries `status: deleted`/`archived: true` — whichever is the actual contract — and the binding store no longer maps the key. State this in the AC table so the test author has no discretion.

findings.finding: The '<10 outbound UPDATE mutations' threshold has no stated rationale for why a non-zero tolerance is correct. The plan's own scrub AC asserts that `prev_snapshot.json` is completely removed; if the scrub succeeds, the expected count should be exactly 0. Using '<10' means up to 9 spurious outbound UPDATE mutations — the precise corruption the plan identifies as the dangerous false-negative for a leftover `prev_snapshot.json` — would not fail the check.
findings.location: Acceptance criteria, dry-run envelope check bullet: 'the first pass plans EXACTLY ZERO deletion mutations AND fewer than 10 outbound UPDATE mutations'
findings.suggested_fix: Change the jq assertion to `jq -e '[.plan[] | select(.direction == "outbound" and .action == "update")] | length == 0'` — if a legitimate non-zero count truly exists, document the exact expected count and its source.

findings.finding: The plan's claim that the '< 10 outbound UPDATE mutations' assertion catches a different scrub failure from the deletion-count assertion — specifically that it independently detects a surviving prev_snapshot.json while the deletion count stays zero — is mechanically incorrect. outbound_differ.compute_outbound_mutations only reaches the UPDATE path for BOUND tickets (jira_key = binding_store.get_jira_key(local_id) is not None; outbound_differ.py:518-530). When bindings.json is deleted by the .bridge_state* glob scrub, get_jira_key returns None for every local ticket, routing all tickets to the outbound CREATE path: zero outbound UPDATEs are produced regardless of whether prev_snapshot.json survives. The '< 10 outbound UPDATEs' check therefore provides no independent protection against a surviving prev_snapshot.json — it passes vacuously whenever bindings.json is correctly deleted. Both assertions catch the same combined failure (both files surviving), not independent failures. An implementer following the plan will believe they have independent coverage of the prev_snapshot.json hazard when they have none.
findings.location: AC block: 'the first pass plans EXACTLY ZERO deletion mutations AND fewer than 10 outbound UPDATE mutations' and 'BOTH are required and they catch DIFFERENT scrub failures: a surviving bindings.json shows up as deletions, while a surviving prev_snapshot.json shows up as spurious outbound UPDATEs'
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the 'BOTH are required and they catch DIFFERENT scrub failures' paragraph with: 'The deletion-count assertion catches a surviving bindings.json (which would attempt to delete production-bound issues from the harness). The UPDATE-count assertion provides a supplemental sanity check but is NOT an independent guard for a surviving prev_snapshot.json — when bindings.json is correctly deleted, no tickets are bound and the outbound UPDATE path is unreachable regardless of prev_snapshot.json. The primary guard for both files is the glob-scrub assertion above; the dry-run counts confirm the scrubbed store is clean but are not a substitute for the glob test.'

findings.finding: The issue-seeding mechanism for the pagination volume test is unspecified — the plan says 'seed at least 2 * observed + 1 issues IN THE HARNESS' but names no method (transport.create_issue? direct REST POST? pytest fixture factory?). Additionally, 'assert the seeded issue count is fully recovered' has no proving command (count of local tickets after inbound pass? a specific log line?).

findings.suggested_fix: State: 'Seed via `transport.create_issue` in a pytest fixture; after the inbound pass assert `recovered_count == seed_count` where `recovered_count` is the number of newly-created tickets in the local store matching the seeded issue keys.'

findings.finding: The pagination AC requires that 'the seeded issue count is FULLY recovered' but provides no proving command. Unlike other ACs in the plan, this claim is stated in prose without a concrete jq filter, count comparison, or output assertion — leaving 'fully recovered' open to interpretation (all seeded issues appear in the inbound plan? in the local store? the count matches the seed count?).
findings.location: Acceptance criteria, pagination bullet: 'assert the seeded issue count is FULLY recovered'

findings.finding: The plan specifies seeding at least `2 * observed + 1` issues in the DC harness container and creating additional issues/links via mutation tests, but defines NO retire/cleanup path for those DC-side objects, and never states whether the container is fresh (ephemeral) per CI run or persistent/reused. If the container is reused across runs or on retry, accumulated DC issues invalidate the pagination assertion (`seeded count == fully recovered count`) and can introduce colliding link/issue state that corrupts mutation assertions. The lifecycle is half-specified: CREATE is described, CONSUME is implied by the test assertions, but RETIRE is absent and the container's freshness contract is unstated.
findings.location: Section 'The DC-side mutation suite', volume bullet: 'seed at least 2 * observed + 1 issues so at least three pages are required'; also Acceptance Criteria bullet on pagination
findings.suggested_fix: Add a setup step in the CI job that either (a) stops and re-starts the Docker container from the base image (guaranteeing a clean slate) or (b) issues a bulk-delete API call to remove all non-default issues before seeding. State explicitly in the plan which approach is used, so the container lifecycle is part of the specified contract rather than an ambient assumption.

findings.finding: The pagination 'fully recovered' assertion has no proving command. The AC states 'the suite seeds at least 2 * observed + 1 issues … Assert the seeded issue count is FULLY recovered' but provides no concrete command (e.g., a count of locally stored issues matching the seeded DC issues) to verify full recovery.
findings.location: AC: '…the suite seeds at least 2 * observed + 1 issues IN THE HARNESS so at least three pages are required … assert the seeded issue count is FULLY recovered'

findings.finding: The pagination test setup (seed 2*observed+1 issues) is correct, but the plan specifies NO assertion that ALL seeded issues actually appear in the local store after the inbound pass. Without an explicit count or membership assertion, a buggy paginator that truncates at page 1 would go undetected: the suite asserts individual round-trips for the mutations it explicitly creates, but those mutations can be placed on page 1, leaving pages 2+ silently unfetched and unverified.
findings.location: AC: 'the suite seeds at least 2 * observed + 1 issues IN THE HARNESS so at least three pages are required'; section 'volume — and note WHAT drives it'
findings.suggested_fix: After the inbound pass, assert `len(local_store.list_tickets()) >= 2 * observed_page_size + 1` (or assert that every seeded issue key appears in the local store). This is the only observable that proves pagination was exercised end-to-end rather than just set up.
